questions.text: The H–F bond enthalpy (568 kJ mol⁻¹) is significantly higher than the H–Cl bond enthalpy (431 kJ mol⁻¹). However, HF is a weaker acid than HCl in aqueous solution. Justify this apparent contradiction using concepts of bond enthalpy and intermolecular forces.
questions.answer_explanation: The high H–F bond enthalpy makes HF less prone to dissociate into H⁺ and F⁻ ions, contributing to its weak acidic nature. Furthermore, in aqueous solution, HF molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which traps the proton and further hinders its release as H₃O⁺. HCl, with a weaker bond and no significant hydrogen bonding in solution, dissociates almost completely.

questions.text: A hydrogen-like species in its excited state emits radiation with a wavelength corresponding to the transition from n=4 to n=2. The same wavelength is observed for the second line of the Balmer series for atomic hydrogen. Identify the species and its atomic number.
questions.answer_explanation: For a hydrogen-like species, 1/λ = RZ²(1/n₁² - 1/n₂²). For the Balmer series of H (Z=1), the second line is n=4→2. Given the same λ, RZ²(1/2² - 1/4²) = R(1)(1/2² - 1/4²). This simplifies to Z² = 1, hence Z=1. The species is He⁺ (helium ion with one electron), which has atomic number 2.

questions.text: For the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = 0, so q = -w. Explain why this simple relationship does not hold for the isothermal free expansion of the same gas into a vacuum, even though both processes start and end at the same temperature.
questions.answer_explanation: In a reversible isothermal expansion, work is done by the gas (w = -nRT ln(V₂/V₁)) and heat is absorbed (q = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)) to maintain constant internal energy. In free expansion into vacuum, no external pressure opposes the gas, so w = 0. Since ΔU = 0 (isothermal, ideal gas), q must also be 0. Therefore, the relationship q = -w (which implies non-zero values) is invalid for free expansion.

questions.text: Although sulfur (S) belongs to Group 16 and has six valence electrons, the octet rule is strictly obeyed in SF₂ but frequently expanded in SF₄ and SF₆. Explain this anomaly by considering the concepts of hybridisation and the availability of low-lying vacant orbitals.
questions.answer_explanation: SF₂ uses sp³ hybridisation of S, accommodating two bonding pairs and two lone pairs within the octet. In SF₄ (sp³d hybridisation) and SF₆ (sp³d² hybridisation), the sulfur atom utilizes its vacant 3d orbitals to form more than four bonds, thereby expanding its octet. This is possible due to the availability of low-lying d-orbitals in the third period.

questions.text: The first ionisation enthalpy of aluminium (577 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of magnesium (738 kJ mol⁻¹), even though Mg has a higher nuclear charge. Justify this observation by analyzing their respective electronic configurations and the stability of the electron being removed.
questions.answer_explanation: Mg has a stable, fully-filled 3s² configuration ([Ne]3s²). Removing an electron disrupts this stability, requiring more energy. Al has the configuration [Ne]3s² 3p¹. The 3p electron is in a higher energy subshell, is partially shielded by the 3s electrons, and is easier to remove, leading to a lower ionisation enthalpy despite the higher nuclear charge.

questions.text: For the reversible reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, ΔH = -92 kJ mol⁻¹. If the volume of the container is suddenly doubled at constant temperature, predict the direction in which the reaction will proceed to re-establish equilibrium. Explain your prediction by linking the change to the reaction quotient Qc.
questions.answer_explanation: Doubling the volume decreases the total pressure and the partial pressure of all gases. Since there are 4 moles of gaseous reactants and 2 moles of gaseous products, the denominator of Qc (in terms of concentration or pressure) decreases more sharply than the numerator. This makes Qc < Kc. To re-establish equilibrium, the reaction will proceed in the forward direction (towards fewer moles of gas) to increase the value of Qc back to Kc.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the mechanism of electrophilic addition in alkenes (e.g., with Br₂) and electrophilic substitution in arenes (e.g., nitration), with specific reference to the role of the π-electron cloud and the formation of the intermediate.
questions.answer_explanation: In alkenes, the π-electron cloud is loosely held and attacks an electrophile (E⁺) directly, forming a carbocation intermediate which is then attacked by a nucleophile. In arenes (benzene), the stable aromatic π-electron cloud donates electron density to the electrophile, forming a resonance-stabilized arenium ion (sigma complex) intermediate. This intermediate loses a proton to regenerate the aromatic ring, completing the substitution, unlike addition which would destroy aromaticity.

questions.text: During the separation of a mixture containing benzoic acid, aniline, and naphthalene using acid-base extraction, a student added NaOH first, followed by HCl. They observed that aniline was extracted into the aqueous layer after the first step. Identify the error in the student's procedure and explain the correct sequence of reagents to isolate all three compounds.
questions.answer_explanation: The error is adding NaOH first. Benzoic acid (acidic) would be deprotonated and extracted into the aqueous layer, but aniline (basic) would remain unionized in the organic layer. The correct sequence is: 1. Add HCl first. Aniline is protonated to form a water-soluble salt and extracted. 2. To the remaining organic layer, add NaOH. Benzoic acid is deprotonated and extracted. 3. Naphthalene (neutral) remains dissolved in the organic solvent throughout.

questions.text: In the reaction: 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 8H₂O + 5Cl₂, identify the species undergoing oxidation and reduction. Calculate the volume of Cl₂(g) produced at STP when 1 mole of KMnO₄ reacts completely with excess HCl.
questions.answer_explanation: Oxidation: Cl⁻ in HCl is oxidized to Cl₂ (O.N. increases from -1 to 0). Reduction: Mn in KMnO₄ is reduced to Mn²⁺ in MnCl₂ (O.N. decreases from +7 to +2). The stoichiometry shows 2 mol KMnO₄ produce 5 mol Cl₂. Therefore, 1 mol KMnO₄ will produce (5/2) = 2.5 mol Cl₂. At STP, volume = 2.5 mol × 22.4 L mol⁻¹ = 56.0 L.

questions.text: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂O. Its vapour density is 30. (i) Determine its molecular formula. (ii) If this compound on complete oxidation yields only CO₂ and H₂O, deduce the total number of sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds present in one molecule of it.
questions.answer_explanation: (i) Vapour density = 30, so molar mass = 2 × VD = 60 g mol⁻¹. Mass of empirical unit (CH₂O) = 30 g mol⁻¹. Therefore, n = 60/30 = 2. Molecular formula = C₂H₄O₂. (ii) Complete oxidation to CO₂ and H₂O suggests it is a carboxylic acid, likely CH₃COOH (acetic acid). Structure: CH₃–C(=O)OH. Total σ bonds: 7 (C–H) + 2 (C–C) + 1 (C–O) + 1 (O–H) + 1 (C=O sigma) = 12 σ bonds. Total π bonds: 1 (in C=O).

questions.text: A student argues that anomalous behaviour of the second-period elements (Li to Ne) when compared to their respective group members is primarily due to their exceptionally small size and high electronegativity. Using specific examples from Groups 1, 2, 13, 14, 16, and 17, critically evaluate this statement. Does this 'anomaly' diminish or follow a pattern as we move down these groups? Substantiate your answer by explaining the underlying periodic properties that govern these trends.
questions.answer_explanation:
1. Evaluate the statement: The student's argument is only partially correct. While small size and high electronegativity are contributing factors, the key reason is the unavailability of d-orbitals for bonding and the high charge-to-radius ratio.
2. Provide contrasting examples across groups:
   - Group 1: Li forms Li₃N, other alkali metals do not; Li₂O is less basic than Na₂O.
   - Group 2: Be shows diagonal relationship with Al, forms covalent compounds (BeCl₂ is polymeric), others are ionic.
   - Group 13: B is a non-metal/metalloid and forms only covalent compounds (BX₃), Al and below show increasing metallic character.
   - Group 14: C forms strong C–C chains (catenation), Si shows less, others negligible; CF₄ is stable while SiF₄ hydrolyses.
   - Group 16: O forms strong hydrogen bonds (H₂O vs H₂S), exists as O₂ gas, others are solids.
   - Group 17: F shows limited covalency (no d-orbitals), forms only one oxoacid (HOF), exhibits atypical electron gain enthalpy.
3. Explain the pattern down the group: Anomalous behaviour diminishes down the group due to increase in size, decrease in electronegativity, availability of d-orbitals (from 3rd period onwards), and decrease in ionisation enthalpy. Behaviour becomes more 'typical' for heavier members.
4. Underlying periodic properties: Ionisation enthalpy, electronegativity, atomic size, and the effect of lanthanoid contraction (for 5th/6th period members) are the governing factors. The concept of 'inert pair effect' also becomes significant for heavier p-block elements.
questions.chapter_tag: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.or_alternative: The first ionization enthalpy (IE₁) of Al (Z=13) is lower than that of Mg (Z=12), but the second ionization enthalpy (IE₂) of Al is significantly higher than that of Mg. Using electronic configurations and the concepts of effective nuclear charge and stability of filled/half-filled subshells, explain this reversal in trend. Furthermore, predict how the trend in IE₁ would continue for Si, P, and S, justifying each prediction based on the same principles.

questions.text: For the gaseous equilibrium: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); ΔH = -92 kJ mol⁻¹. Initially, 1 mole of N₂ and 3 moles of H₂ are taken in a 1 L sealed container at 400 K. At equilibrium, the total pressure is found to be P₁. Now, the temperature is increased to 500 K, and a new equilibrium is established with total pressure P₂ (P₂ > P₁). A student claims that because the reaction is exothermic, increasing temperature should favour the reverse reaction, decreasing the yield of NH₃, and this should logically lead to an increase in the total number of moles, hence P₂ should be greater than P₁. However, another student argues that if the equilibrium constant Kₚ decreases with temperature, the partial pressures of reactants must increase, but the effect on total pressure is not straightforward. Analyse this scenario step-by-step. Derive the relationship between Kₚ and the extent of reaction (ξ). Using Le Chatelier's principle and the mathematical expression for Kₚ, determine whether P₂ will always be greater than P₁ for any exothermic reaction when volume is fixed. What other factor, besides the shift in equilibrium, critically influences the final pressure P₂?
questions.answer_explanation:
1. Initial moles: n_N₂ = 1, n_H₂ = 3, n_NH₃ = 0. Let ξ be the extent of reaction (moles of N₂ reacted). At equilibrium: n_N₂ = 1-ξ, n_H₂ = 3-3ξ, n_NH₃ = 2ξ. Total moles, n_total = 4 - 2ξ.
2. Relationship with Kₚ: Kₚ = (P_NH₃)² / (P_N₂ * (P_H₂)³). Since P_i = (n_i / n_total) * P_total. Therefore, Kₚ = [(2ξ/(4-2ξ))² * P_total²] / [((1-ξ)/(4-2ξ)) * ((3-3ξ)/(4-2ξ))³ * P_total⁴]. Simplifies to Kₚ = [4ξ²(4-2ξ)²] / [27(1-ξ)⁴ * P_total²]. Shows Kₚ ∝ 1/P_total² for a given ξ.
3. Effect of Temperature Increase:
   - For exothermic reaction, Kₚ decreases with increase in T.
   - From the expression, if Kₚ decreases, for the same initial conditions, either ξ must decrease or P_total must increase, or both.
   - Le Chatelier: Increase in T favours endothermic (reverse) reaction, ξ decreases. This increases n_total (since n_total = 4 - 2ξ, and ξ decreases).
4. Pressure Change Analysis: P_total = (n_total * R * T) / V. Two factors change: n_total increases (because ξ decreases) and T increases. Both factors act to increase P_total. Therefore, P₂ > P₁ is inevitable for this specific reaction in a fixed volume.
5. Generalisation and the Other Critical Factor: For any gas-phase exothermic reaction where Δn_g < 0 (like here, Δn_g = -2), an increase in T will always increase P_total in a fixed volume because both the increase in T and the increase in n_total (due to equilibrium shift towards more moles) work synergistically. The other critical factor is the direct, non-equilibrium effect of temperature on pressure via the Ideal Gas Law (P ∝ T). Even if the equilibrium composition didn't change, P would increase with T.

A solution is prepared by dissolving sodium salt NaHA in water. Derive an expression for the pH of this solution, clearly stating the assumptions made. Now, if a small amount of strong acid (HCl) is added to this NaHA solution, will the pH change be minimal (acting as a buffer) or significant? Justify by analysing which equilibrium (the first or the second dissociation of H₂A) is primarily responsible for the buffering action in a NaHA solution. How does the relative magnitude of Kₐ₁ and Kₐ₂ affect this conclusion?

questions.text: An unknown hydrocarbon 'X' with molecular formula C₇H₁₂ does not decolorise bromine in CCl₄ in the dark but does so rapidly in sunlight. It reacts with exactly 2 equivalents of H₂ in the presence of Lindlar's catalyst to give compound 'Y'. However, when 'X' is treated with sodium in liquid ammonia, it yields a different compound 'Z'. Both 'Y' and 'Z' are isomers with formula C₇H₁₄. Upon vigorous oxidation with hot acidic KMnO₄, 'X' yields a mixture of three different carboxylic acids. Deduce the exact structure of 'X'. Provide a detailed reaction pathway showing the formation of 'Y' and 'Z' from 'X' with mechanisms/conditions. Explain the stereochemical outcomes (cis/trans) of the reactions with Lindlar's catalyst and Na/NH₃(l) and how these, combined with the ozonolysis-like oxidation products, allow unambiguous structural determination.
questions.answer_explanation:
1. Analysing Molecular Formula: C₇H₁₂. Degree of Unsaturation = [(2×7 + 2) - 12]/2 = 4. This indicates either four double bonds, three double bonds + one ring, two double bonds + two rings, one triple bond + two double bonds, etc.
2. Interpreting Tests:
   - No reaction with Br₂/CCl₄ in dark but reaction in sunlight suggests an alkane substitution under sunlight (free radical) is possible, but the key is no electrophilic addition in dark. This is characteristic of an alkyne, which reacts slowly with Br₂. The rapid reaction in sunlight is free radical addition.
   - Lindlar's catalyst (poisoned Pd) leads to syn addition of H₂, giving cis-alkene 'Y'.
   - Na/NH₃(l) leads to dissolving metal reduction, giving trans-alkene 'Z' via anti addition.
   - Both 'Y' and 'Z' are C₇H₁₄, confirming addition of 2H₂ (4H atoms) to 'X', meaning 'X' has one triple bond (accounts for 2 unsaturations) and two other unsaturations (likely two rings or one ring and one double bond).
3. Oxidation Product Analysis: Vigorous oxidation cleaves at multiple unsaturation points. Formation of three different carboxylic acids indicates the triple bond and other unsaturations are internal, not terminal, and the molecule is symmetrical or has distinct cleavage points. A likely candidate is a cyclic alkyne or an alkyne with rings.
4. Deduced Structure: Given C₇ chain, one triple bond, and the need for symmetry to give three acids, a symmetrical cycloalkyne with a 7-membered ring is unstable (angle strain). A more plausible structure is 1,2-Dimethylcyclopent-1-en-3-yne. However, a better fit for three acids and the H₂ addition results is 3-Heptyne (CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃) would give only two acids (propanoic and butanoic). To get three acids, the triple bond must be between carbons that are not symmetrically substituted, and there must be another point of unsaturation (a double bond or ring) that gets cleaved. A definitive structure meeting all criteria: 4-Methylhex-2-en-4-yne is unlikely. The logical structure is a conjugated enyne with a specific substitution pattern. Example: CH₂=CH–C≡C–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (Hept-1-en-3-yne). Oxidation would give HCOOH (from CH₂=), (COOH)₂ from –C≡C–, and CH₃CH₂COOH. That's three acids.
5. Stereochemical Outcomes:
   - Lindlar's: Syn addition to triple bond gives cis double bond in the alkene part of 'Y'.
   - Na/NH₃: Anti addition via radical anions gives trans double bond in 'Z'.
6. Unambiguous Determination: The combination defines the position of the triple bond and the geometry of the resulting alkenes, while the oxidation products identify the carbon skeleton and substituent positions.
questions.or_alternative: Two isomeric hydrocarbons A and B, both with molecular formula C₆H₁₀, undergo catalytic hydrogenation to yield the same straight-chain alkane C₆H₁₄. questions.source_text: A student was investigating the concept of resonance in polyatomic ions. The carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻) was taken as a case study. The standard Lewis structure shows one carbon-oxygen double bond and two carbon-oxygen single bonds, implying two different C–O bond lengths. However, experimental evidence from X-ray diffraction studies shows that all three C–O bonds in the carbonate ion are identical in length, measuring 128 pm. This length is intermediate between a typical C–O single bond (≈143 pm) and a C=O double bond (≈122 pm). This phenomenon cannot be explained by a single static Lewis structure.
questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the following questions:

sub_questions.text: What fundamental limitation of the Lewis dot structure approach does the case of the carbonate ion highlight?
sub_questions.answer_explanation: A single Lewis structure fails to accurately represent molecules/ions where the bonding is delocalised. It suggests localized single and double bonds, which contradicts experimental evidence of equivalent bonds.

sub_questions.text: Explain the concept that is used to accurately describe the bonding in the carbonate ion, and how it accounts for the observed identical bond lengths.
sub_questions.answer_explanation: The concept is resonance. The actual structure of CO₃²⁻ is a resonance hybrid of three equivalent canonical forms. In each form, the double bond is located between C and a different O atom. The hybrid is an average of these structures, resulting in a bond order of approximately 1.33 and identical bond lengths for all three C–O bonds.

sub_questions.text: If one were to predict the C–O bond length in the formate ion (HCOO⁻) based on this understanding, would you expect the two C–O bonds to be of equal or different lengths? Justify briefly.
sub_questions.answer_explanation: The two C–O bonds in the formate ion (HCOO⁻) would be expected to be of equal length. This is because the negative charge is delocalised over the two oxygen atoms, making the two C–O bonds equivalent through resonance between the two canonical structures.

questions.text: Given the successive ionization enthalpies (in kJ mol⁻¹) of an element: IE₁ = 419, IE₂ = 3051, IE₃ = 4412, IE₄ = 5877. Predict the group number of this element in the periodic table and its most probable stable ionic state.
questions.answer_explanation: The large jump between IE₁ and IE₂ indicates easy removal of the first electron, characteristic of Group 1 elements. The stable ion would be X⁺.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), increasing pressure by adding an inert gas at constant volume does not shift the equilibrium.
Reason (R): The partial pressures of the reacting gases remain unchanged when an inert gas is added at constant volume.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is true but R is false
options.d: A is false but R is true

questions.answer_explanation: At constant volume, adding an inert gas increases total pressure but not partial pressures. Since equilibrium constant Kp depends on partial pressures, there is no shift.

questions.text: Study the diagram above showing radial probability distribution (4πr²R²) vs. distance (r) plots for an electron in a hydrogenic system. The plots have two peaks: a major peak at a larger distance and a smaller, sharper peak very close to the nucleus. Which orbital does this represent, and what is the significance of the inner peak?
questions.image_prompt: A graph with x-axis labeled 'r (distance from nucleus)' and y-axis labeled 'Radial Probability (4πr²R²)'. Two curves are shown: a dotted line with a single broad peak and a solid line with a sharp peak close to the origin followed by a much larger, broader peak at a greater distance.

options.a: 2s orbital; the inner peak indicates a radial node where probability density is zero.
options.b: 2p orbital; the inner peak indicates maximum probability density at the nucleus.
options.c: 3s orbital; the inner peak represents a region of non-zero probability density very close to the nucleus.
options.d: 1s orbital; the inner peak is an artifact and has no physical significance.

questions.answer_explanation: The plot with two peaks is characteristic of ns orbitals with n≥2. The small inner peak indicates a finite probability of finding the electron very close to the nucleus, a feature absent in p, d orbitals.

questions.text: A mixture of 0.1 mol of N₂ and 0.3 mol of H₂ is allowed to reach equilibrium with NH₃ in a 1 L vessel. At equilibrium, the total pressure is P atm and the mole fraction of NH₃ is 0.2. The equilibrium constant Kp for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is expressed in terms of P. Which expression is correct?
questions.answer_explanation: Mole fraction of NH₃ = 0.2, so its partial pressure = 0.2P. For N₂ and H₂, mole fractions are 0.2 and 0.6 respectively. Kp = (p_NH₃)²/(p_N₂ * p_H₂³) = (0.2P)²/(0.2P * (0.6P)³) = (0.04)/(0.2*(0.6)³) * P⁻².

questions.text: A compound C₅H₁₀O₂ upon treatment with NaHCO₃ liberates CO₂. Its IR spectrum shows a strong, broad absorption around 3000 cm⁻¹ and a sharp peak at 1715 cm⁻¹. Its ¹H NMR shows a singlet at δ 2.1 (3H), a quartet at δ 4.1 (2H), and a triplet at δ 1.3 (3H). Which reaction sequence would NOT be a valid synthesis for this compound?

options.a: Oxidation of pentan-2-ol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.
options.b: Esterification of ethanoic acid with propan-1-ol.
options.c: Hydrolysis of ethyl propanoate with aqueous NaOH.
options.d: Reaction of propanoic acid with ethanol in presence of conc. H₂SO₄.

questions.answer_explanation: The data indicates ethyl acetate (CH₃COOC₂H₅). Hydrolysis of ethyl propanoate (C₂H₅COOC₂H₅) would yield propanoic acid and ethanol, not ethyl acetate.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): In the titration of a weak acid (HA) with a strong base (NaOH), the pH at the equivalence point is always greater than 7.
Reason (R): At the equivalence point, the salt formed (NaA) hydrolyzes to produce OH⁻ ions, making the solution basic.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is true but R is false
options.d: A is false but R is true

questions.answer_explanation: For a weak acid-strong base titration, the salt of the conjugate base (A⁻) undergoes hydrolysis: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻, resulting in a pH > 7.

questions.text: If 2.0 g of a mixture of NaHCO₃ and Na₂CO₃ required 40 mL of 1.0 M HCl for complete neutralization using phenolphthalein indicator, and then a further 15 mL of the same acid using methyl orange indicator to reach the second endpoint, the mass percentage of Na₂CO₃ in the mixture is closest to:
questions.answer_explanation: Phenolphthalein endpoint: moles HCl = moles of Na₂CO₃ (since it neutralizes to NaHCO₃). Methyl orange (additional): moles HCl = moles of NaHCO₃ (from original + from first step). Solving gives mass of Na₂CO₃ ≈ 1.323 g in 2.0 g mixture → ~66.2%.

questions.text: When ethene is passed through a dilute, cold, aqueous solution of KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent), it forms ethane-1,2-diol. In this reaction, the change in the oxidation state of manganese and the role of ethene are, respectively:
questions.answer_explanation: KMnO₄ (Mn in +7) is reduced to MnO₂ (Mn in +4) in cold, dilute conditions. Ehene (CH₂=CH₂) is oxidized to the diol (CH₂OH-CH₂OH), gaining two -OH groups.

questions.text: Consider the molecular orbital configuration for a homonuclear diatomic molecule: (σ1s)² (σ*1s)² (σ2s)² (σ*2s)² (σ2pz)² (π2px)² (π2py)² (π*2px)¹. The bond order and magnetic character of this species are:
questions.answer_explanation: Bond order = (Nb - Na)/2 = (10 - 7)/2 = 1.5. Presence of unpaired electron(s) (in π*2px) makes it paramagnetic.

questions.text: In the reaction 3Br₂ + 6OH⁻ → 5Br⁻ + BrO₃⁻ + 3H₂O, which statement correctly describes the fate of bromine?

options.c: Some bromine atoms are oxidized from 0 to +5, others are reduced from 0 to -1.
options.d: Bromine undergoes disproportionation, but the oxidation state changes are from 0 to -1 and 0 to -5.

questions.answer_explanation: This is a disproportionation reaction. In BrO₃⁻, Br is in +5 state (oxidized). In Br⁻, Br is in -1 state (reduced). The starting Br₂ has oxidation state 0.

questions.text: An alkane (A), C₆H₁₄, on monochlorination gives a single constitutional isomer of the chloroalkane (B). (B) on treatment with alcoholic KOH yields an alkene (C) which, on ozonolysis followed by Zn/H₂O treatment, yields only propanone (CH₃COCH₃). The structure of (A) is:
questions.answer_explanation: Only 2,2-dimethylbutane (neopentane-like structure) gives a single monochlorination product (tertiary chloride). Dehydrohalogenation yields a tetrasubstituted alkene which on reductive ozonolysis gives two moles of acetone.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): The second ionization enthalpy of magnesium (Mg) is greater than that of aluminum (Al).
Reason (R): For Mg⁺, the electron is removed from a fully filled 3s subshell, while for Al⁺, it is removed from a half-filled 3p subshell which is more stable.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is true but R is false
options.d: A is false but R is true

questions.answer_explanation: A is true: IE₂(Mg) > IE₂(Al). R is false because the reason is inverted; Mg⁺ has config [Ne]3s¹, removing from a half-filled s orbital is not easier. Al⁺ has config [Ne]3s², removing from a filled s orbital is harder, but the actual IE₂ order is due to the higher effective nuclear charge on Mg⁺.

questions.text: For the process H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 100°C and 1 atm pressure, which of the following combinations is correct? (ΔH_vap is enthalpy of vaporization)
questions.answer_explanation: At boiling point (100°C, 1 atm), the process is at equilibrium, so ΔG = 0. Vaporization is endothermic and increases disorder, so ΔS > 0. ΔH_vap = ΔU + PΔV, and since PΔV > 0 for expansion, ΔU < ΔH_vap.

questions.text: In the separation of a mixture containing benzoic acid, aniline, and naphthalene by solvent extraction, the correct sequence of reagents to be added to the ether solution to isolate the components one by one is:

options.a: Dil. HCl, then dil. NaOH, then water.
options.b: Dil. NaOH, then dil. HCl, then water.
options.c: Dil. NaHCO₃, then dil. HCl, then dil. NaOH.
options.d: Dil. HCl, then dil. NaHCO₃, then dil. NaOH.

questions.answer_explanation: First, add dil. HCl to convert basic aniline into its water-soluble salt (anilinium chloride). Extract. Then add dil. NaHCO₃ to convert benzoic acid into water-soluble sodium benzoate (CO₂ evolution confirms). Extract. Naphthalene remains in ether.

questions.text: A 0.05 M aqueous solution of a salt MX₂ has an observed freezing point depression of 0.12 K. Given Kf for water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹, the approximate percentage dissociation of the salt and the van't Hoff factor (i) are:
questions.answer_explanation: ΔTf = i * Kf * m. 0.12 = i * 1.86 * 0.05 → i ≈ 1.29. For MX₂ → M²⁺ + 2X⁻, α = (i-1)/(n-1) = (1.29-1)/(3-1) = 0.29/2 = 0.145 or ~15%. Closest given is 50% with i=1.5 (which would give ΔTf=0.1395K ≈ 0.12K considering approximations).

questions.text:
Assertion (A): The O–H bond length in water (H₂O) is shorter than the O–H bond length in methanol (CH₃OH).
Reason (R): The oxygen atom in water is sp³ hybridized, while in methanol it is sp² hybridized, leading to a longer bond in methanol due to lower s-character.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is true but R is false
options.d: A is false but R is true

questions.answer_explanation: A is false; O-H bond length in water (~96 pm) is typically longer than in methanol (~94 pm) due to stronger hydrogen bonding in water affecting electron distribution. R is also false; oxygen in both water and methanol is approximately sp³ hybridized.
